opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a lot of hard problems simply aren't solvable in one shot. If you asked a person to read a tricky math olympiad problem and blurt out the answer immediately, even a very strong mathematician would usually fail. What makes them succeed is the ability to sit with the problem: try an approach, notice it isn't working, back up, test small cases, form a conjecture, check it, and eventually assemble a proof. More inference-time compute gives a model room to do that same kind of exploration.

So one benefit is depth. The model can carry a line of reasoning further, keep track of more intermediate steps, and catch its own mistakes before committing to an answer. Another is breadth. It can consider several strategies instead of locking onto the first idea that comes to mind. And maybe most importantly, it can verify. On problems where checking is easier than generating, spending extra thought on "is this actually right?" makes a huge difference in reliability.

What's been exciting is seeing that this scales. As we let models think for longer, from seconds to minutes and now to much longer horizons, performance on genuinely difficult reasoning tasks keeps improving. That suggests the gains don't come only from making the model bigger or giving it more training data. They also come from letting it use its capabilities more deliberately at the moment it's solving a problem. For me, that's a really meaningful shift. It means we can trade time for quality, much as people do, and it opens the door to models working on problems where the answer isn't already somewhere in the training distribution and has to be worked out.

r001.rationale: The response says extra inference time gives the model room to explore approaches, check its reasoning, and catch mistakes before committing to an answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there are really two axes along which you can scale a model. The one everyone's been focused on for years is training compute: bigger models, more data, longer pretraining runs. And that works, but it's expensive and slow, and you only get to pay that cost once, up front, before you know what question anyone is going to ask.

Inference-time compute is the other axis. It's letting the model think longer at the moment it's actually faced with a problem. And the thing that makes that powerful is that not all problems are equally hard. If you ask a model what the capital of France is, it should just answer. If you ask it to prove a competition math problem, or debug something subtle in a large codebase, the right amount of effort is wildly different. A fixed forward pass can't adapt to that. A model that can reason for longer can.

The analogy I keep coming back to is how people actually work. When I was doing math competitions, nobody was good because they instantly saw the answer. They were good because they could sit with a problem for a long time, try an approach, notice it wasn't working, back up, try something else, check their work. That process of exploration and self-correction is where most of the value is, and that's exactly what you unlock when you give a model room to think.

There's also a practical benefit: it gives you a dial. Instead of needing a different model for every capability level, you can trade latency and cost for quality on a per-query basis. For a lot of applications, that's a much better deal than retraining.

And the part I find most exciting is that these two axes compound. A model that's been trained to use its thinking time well gets more out of each additional unit of compute than one that hasn't. So you train it to reason, and then you let it reason longer, and the gains stack. We're still pretty early in understanding how far that goes, but every time we've pushed on it, the curve has kept going.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can spend longer exploring approaches, back up, try another, and check its work before answering, communicating that extra inference-time compute lets it refine its answer before giving a final output.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as giving the model more time to work through a problem before it answers. Some questions you can answer immediately, but others benefit from trying an approach, checking whether it works, and revising it if it doesn’t. More inference-time compute gives a model room to do that.

That’s a different lever from making the model larger or training it longer. You can take the same trained model and spend more computation on a particular question. Ideally, you spend very little on an easy question and more on a difficult one.

The caveat is that more time doesn’t automatically produce a better answer. The model has to use that computation productively. But when it can, you get a way to trade additional latency and cost for better performance on harder problems.

r001.rationale: The response says extra compute gives the model time to try an approach, check whether it works, and revise it before answering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is that you’re giving the model more time to think before it answers. There are lots of problems where the first thing that comes to mind isn’t right, but if you can work through the details, try a different approach, or check your work, you can do much better.

Inference-time compute gives a model room to do those things. Instead of having to produce an answer immediately, it can spend computation reasoning through the problem. And that gives us another way to improve performance beyond training a bigger model: we can take the same model and let it work longer on a difficult question.

The important caveat is that more computation isn’t automatically useful. The model has to have learned how to use that extra time productively. But when it has, you can trade off speed and cost against the quality of the answer, depending on what the task needs.

r001.rationale: It explains that extra inference-time computation gives the model time to reason, try another approach, and check its work before answering.
